decisions.title: Keep all data on the phone with SQLite
decisions.problem: The app needed working accounts, rooms, bookings and feedback that survive closing the app, without setting up and paying for a server.
alternatives: A cloud backend such as Firebase
Android's Room persistence library on top of SQLite
decisions.decision: All data lives in a local SQLite database, accessed through one SQLiteOpenHelper class with hand-written SQL.
tradeoffs: Works offline and needs no server, accounts or network permission
Writing the SQL by hand shows exactly how tables and queries work, but needs more code than Room
Each phone has its own database, so students on different phones do not see each other's bookings; a real deployment needs a shared backend
evidence: DatabaseHelper extends SQLiteOpenHelper and creates studyusia.db
The manifest requests no permissions, including internet access
Schema upgrades drop and recreate the tables (database version 9)

decisions.title: Check for clashes before a booking is saved
decisions.problem: Two students must not hold the same room at the same time, and rooms can only be booked during their opening hours and available dates.
alternatives: A unique key on room, date and start time (only catches identical start times, not partial overlaps)
Pre-generated time slots in the schedules table
decisions.decision: Before a booking is made, isRoomAvailable checks the room's date range and opening hours, then queries for any confirmed booking that overlaps the requested time.
tradeoffs: Students can choose any start and end time instead of fixed slots
The rule lives in app code, not the schema, so every path that saves a booking must call it
Touching bookings count as a clash, so 12:00–14:00 cannot follow 10:00–12:00
Dates and times are compared as text, which works because the pickers always save zero-padded YYYY-MM-DD and HH:MM
evidence: DatabaseHelper.isRoomAvailable: three overlap conditions on start_time and end_time
Called from NewBookingScreen and from the Room Availability search
Run the AV scenarios in the Testing tab

decisions.title: Protect room management with an admin key
decisions.problem: Students should book rooms, but only staff should be able to create, change or delete them.
alternatives: An admin role stored on each user account
A separate admin app or web dashboard
decisions.decision: Create, update and delete room screens ask for an admin access key before saving.
tradeoffs: Simple to build and easy to demonstrate
The key is shared and built into the app, so anyone who learns it can manage rooms
Like sign-in, this is prototype-level security: a production version needs admin roles on accounts and hashed passwords
evidence: CreateRoom.kt and UpdateRoom.kt check the key before addRoom, updateRoom and deleteRoom
The users table has no role column

decisions.title: Use readable IDs such as BK001
decisions.problem: Bookings, rooms and users needed identifiers that are easy to read on screen and when checking the database.
decisions.decision: Each table uses a text primary key made of a prefix and a three-digit number (USR001, RM001, BK001, FB001). generateId reads the highest existing ID and adds one.
tradeoffs: IDs are easy to read and to quote, for example when talking about a booking
Creating a record needs an extra query first

The number is read from the fourth character onwards, which fits three-letter prefixes such as USR; for two-letter prefixes such as RM and BK, the ID after BK100 would come out as BK001 again and clash
evidence: All five tables use TEXT PRIMARY KEY columns
